_README: Research-confirmed facts about places the automated sources can't see.
The GIS layers only know what someone has mapped. A town park with no
OpenStreetMap trail tagged inside it comes out 'unverified' even when a
single web search proves it has trails, parking and a pavilion. This file
is where that human research lands.
Entries are matched on name + town and applied AFTER the automated pass,
so they override it. Every entry must carry `source` and `checked` — a
claim without a citation is a guess, and guesses are what this file
exists to replace.
Fields you can set: trails, parking, water, waterName, waterType, sports,
sportList, playground, historic, beach, pool, dogpark, fee, url, note,
agency, acres.
`rules` entries match on type/subtype/agency instead of a single name, so one cited regulation can settle hundreds of places at once. Same requirement: source and checked date.
THIS FILE IS NEVER REGENERATED. places.json is rebuilt from scratch every
month and anything typed into it is destroyed; this file is the only place
in the pipeline meant to be edited by hand, and the workflow's commit step
names its files explicitly so it can never touch this one.
Add `at: [lat, lng]` to any match block. Names change upstream — a source
re-spells a park and the entry silently stops applying — but locations
don't. If the name lookup fails, the nearest place within 600 m wins, so
the research survives the rename.
Every run writes data/research-audit.json, and the workflow fails if any
entry or rule matched nothing. That failure is deliberate: research going
quietly missing is invisible in the output, because the output still looks
perfectly fine without it.

places.note: Roughly 100 acres of town open space at 158 Town Farm Road. Hiking and unmarked trails, a pond, and a reservable pavilion with picnic tables and grills. Leashed dogs welcome.

places.rename: Lucius Pond Ordway – Devil's Den Preserve
places.note: 1,746 acres across Weston and Redding — the largest preserve in Fairfield County, with a 20-mile trail system. Open dawn to dusk. Main parking at the end of Pent Road, Weston; small pull-off on Dayton Road, Redding.
Part of the Devil's Den preserve complex. Open dawn to dusk; trail maps at the Pent Road parking area in Weston.

siteRules: Dogs must be leashed (7 ft max)
No motor vehicles off designated roads
rules.why: Connecticut state parks, forests and wildlife management areas are open to the public daily from 8am to sunset by regulation. Walking is permitted throughout, so state land does not need a mapped trail to be reachable.

siteRules: Open 8am to sunset; closed half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise
rules.why: Conn. Agencies Regs. 26-16-3a governs public use of state wildlife management areas. Hiking is permitted; these are working conservation land rather than developed parks.
Municipal and non-profit burying grounds are walk-in public space during daylight. They are not required to have a mapped trail to be visitable.

siteRules: Some preserves restricted for nesting or fragile habitat — check posted signs
rules.why: Avalonia's 46 preserves, over 5,000 acres across nine southeastern Connecticut towns, are open and free to the public dawn to dusk, with trail maps online and posted on site.

siteRules: Some preserves allow bikes or horses — check the preserve page
rules.why: Over 7,500 acres in northeast Connecticut, with about 18 hikeable properties and 16+ miles of trails open to the public. Note: not every Wyndham holding is trailed, so this asserts reachable rather than claiming a trail on each parcel.

siteRules: Open dawn to dusk, year round
rules.why: Flanders manages over 2,400 acres in Woodbury and neighbouring towns. Trails at its seven major preserves are open to the public at no charge, dawn to dusk, year round.
45 trailed nature preserves across Easton, Weston, Westport, Fairfield, Southport, Norwalk and Bridgeport, all open to walk dawn to dusk.

siteRules: Town open space, open to residents and visitors
rules.why: Glastonbury publishes an inventory and map of its town-owned open spaces, many with walking trails. Municipal open space in Connecticut is public; the town cannot exclude non-residents.

siteRules: Passive recreation: hiking, birding, nature study
A few preserves are closed to protect at-risk species — check before visiting
rules.why: Most TNC Connecticut preserves are open free for low-impact recreation. Deliberately not claiming trails, because TNC states some preserves harbouring at-risk species are closed.

siteRules: Municipal open space, open to residents and non-residents alike
rules.why: Land recorded in PAD-US as city or town owned is municipal open space. Under Leydon v. Greenwich (2001) a Connecticut municipality may not close its parks and open space to non-residents, so this land is public by law.
